items.prompt: What is the difference between WCAG conformance levels A, AA, and AAA?
choices: They apply to different content types (A for text, AA for images, AAA for video)
A, AA, and AAA are three increasingly strict bars — A is the minimum, AAA the strictest
AAA is for mobile apps and A/AA are for desktop websites only
They're just alternate names for the same requirements, chosen per country
items.explanation: A, AA, and AAA are ordered strictness levels of the same guidelines — AAA includes stricter versions of many AA criteria (e.g. a 7:1 contrast ratio instead of 4.5:1), not a different topic area.
items.reference:
A
minimum
AA
common target
AAA
strictest

Why: each level is a stricter bar than the last; most orgs target AA.

items.prompt: Most organizations target WCAG level AA rather than AAA site-wide. Why?
choices: AA criteria are mostly checkable with automated contrast and markup scanners, so teams assume AAA would demand slow, expensive manual testing for every page
AAA doesn't apply to websites, only to native mobile apps
AAA criteria were designed around mobile touchscreen and gesture input, so desktop sites and automated pipelines default to targeting AA instead
AA is the tier referenced by public-sector procurement rules specifically, so private companies only adopt it when bidding on government contracts
items.explanation: AA is the widely-referenced legal/industry bar. AAA is stricter in ways that can be genuinely hard to satisfy everywhere (e.g. 7:1 contrast for all text), so it's usually reserved for specific high-stakes content rather than an entire site.
items.reference:
A
minimum
AA
common target
AAA
strictest

Why: each level is a stricter bar than the last; most orgs target AA.

items.prompt: A criterion requires every image to have alternative text. Which WCAG conformance level does a criterion this fundamental belong to?
choices: AAA, since it's the strictest tier
AA, since it's the common target
A, since without it some users are completely blocked
None — alt text is a best practice, not a WCAG criterion
items.explanation: Level A covers the most basic, foundational barriers — the kind that completely block some users if missing. Alternative text for images is a Level A criterion for exactly that reason.
items.reference:
A
minimum
AA
common target
AAA
strictest

Why: each level is a stricter bar than the last; most orgs target AA.

items.prompt: A dropdown menu only opens on mouse `hover`, with no keyboard equivalent. Which POUR principle does this fail?
choices: Perceivable
Operable
Understandable
Robust
items.explanation: Operable asks 'can it be used without a mouse, or without fine motor control?' A hover-only interaction has no keyboard path, so keyboard-only and many screen reader users can never open it.
items.reference:
👁️ Perceivable
⌨️ Operable
🧭 Understandable
🛠️ Robust

Why: an interface needs all four at once — none substitutes for another.

items.prompt: A custom checkbox is built from a styled `<div>` that no screen reader recognizes as a checkbox at all. Which POUR principle does this fail most directly?
choices: Perceivable
Operable
Understandable
Robust
items.explanation: Robust asks whether the interface keeps working correctly across browsers and assistive technology. A custom control with no recognizable role breaks down specifically when different assistive tech tries to interpret it.
items.reference:
👁️ Perceivable
⌨️ Operable
🧭 Understandable
🛠️ Robust

Why: an interface needs all four at once — none substitutes for another.

items.prompt: A user with a tremor that makes precise pointing difficult falls into which disability category discussed in L1?
choices: Visual
Auditory
Motor
Cognitive
items.explanation: Motor disabilities affect fine motor control and precise pointing — the design response is full keyboard operability, larger click/tap targets, and avoiding strict time limits.
items.reference:
CategoryNeeds
VisualText alternatives, contrast, no color-only meaning
AuditoryCaptions, transcripts, visual alerts
MotorFull keyboard access, large targets, no strict timers
CognitiveClear language, predictable navigation

items.prompt: An error message that says only 'Invalid input,' with no hint what's actually wrong, is a barrier primarily for which category of need?
choices: Visual
Auditory
Motor
Cognitive
items.explanation: Cognitive needs include predictable, clear communication. A vague, unhelpful error message doesn't block seeing or clicking anything — it blocks understanding what to do next, which is a cognitive/comprehension barrier.
items.reference:
CategoryNeeds
VisualText alternatives, contrast, no color-only meaning
AuditoryCaptions, transcripts, visual alerts
MotorFull keyboard access, large targets, no strict timers
CognitiveClear language, predictable navigation

items.prompt: A video with no captions and no transcript excludes users in which category most directly?
choices: Visual
Auditory
Motor
Cognitive
items.explanation: Auditory needs require a non-audio way to access audio content. Captions and transcripts are exactly that — without them, a deaf or hard-of-hearing user has no way to get the video's content.
items.reference:
CategoryNeeds
VisualText alternatives, contrast, no color-only meaning
AuditoryCaptions, transcripts, visual alerts
MotorFull keyboard access, large targets, no strict timers
CognitiveClear language, predictable navigation

items.prompt: Why does 'we'll add accessibility later' tend to fail structurally, not just in practice, per L1?
choices: Because accessibility compliance laws are typically scoped to newly launched products, so an existing product can legally defer fixes until its next redesign
Because it's usually dozens of small decisions baked into markup and layout from day one, not one feature that can be added afterward
Because screen reader and assistive-tech testing tools are only reliable against a fully deployed production build, not against work still in development
Because accessibility requirements are written into procurement law for government and public-sector websites, and don't bind ordinary commercial products
items.explanation: Accessibility is mostly a property of many individual decisions (is this a button or a div, does this color pass contrast, does this modal trap focus) made throughout a build — retrofitting means reopening each one later, under a deadline nobody planned for.
items.reference:
🧱 Dozens of small decisions baked into markup, not one feature
💸 Retrofitting reopens shipped components under deadline
👥 1B+ people with disabilities, plus situational/temporary limits

Why: the cost isn't the individual fix, it's re-opening decisions already considered final.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does the framing 'it's for a small number of users' undercount the actual need for accessible design?
choices: It doesn't undercount anything — accessibility genuinely affects a narrow, fixed population of permanently disabled users that doesn't meaningfully grow over time
Because over a billion people live with some form of disability, before even counting situational or temporary limitations like a sprained wrist or glare on a screen
Because the guidelines were written specifically for school and university websites serving disabled students under 18, not general commercial products
Because most disabilities are effectively resolved by modern assistive technology, so interface-level accommodations have become largely redundant
items.explanation: L1 cites WHO's estimate of over a billion people with some disability, and notes the same design choices also help situational and temporary cases — a broken arm, bright sunlight glare, a slow connection — which is a much larger population than 'permanent disability' alone.
items.reference:
🧱 Dozens of small decisions baked into markup, not one feature
💸 Retrofitting reopens shipped components under deadline
👥 1B+ people with disabilities, plus situational/temporary limits

Why: the cost isn't the individual fix, it's re-opening decisions already considered final.

items.prompt: A screen reader user tabs through a checkout page and hears only 'button' for the close control, with no further information. What was missing?
choices: The button's CSS hover style
An accessible name for the button
The button's page position
The page's meta description
items.explanation: A screen reader announces role and accessible name. With no text, no aria-label, and only an icon inside, the button has a role but no name — so only 'button' gets announced.
items.reference:
🔊 Screen reader — reads the accessibility tree aloud
🕹️ Switch device — single/few-button navigation
🗣️ Voice control — spoken commands to operate the UI

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of assistive technology, as discussed in L1?
choices: A CSS framework
A screen reader
A build pipeline
A CDN
items.explanation: A screen reader is assistive technology — software that reads the accessibility tree aloud (or to a braille display) for a user who can't rely on visually scanning the screen.
items.reference:
🔊 Screen reader — reads the accessibility tree aloud
🕹️ Switch device — single/few-button navigation
🗣️ Voice control — spoken commands to operate the UI

items.prompt: A user who cannot use a standard mouse or keyboard operates a page with a small number of physical buttons that step through focusable elements one at a time. What is this an example of?
choices: A keyboard shortcut
A switch device
A voice assistant
A screen magnifier
items.explanation: A switch device lets someone navigate and activate controls using one or a few physical switches, stepping through focusable elements — it relies on the same underlying focus order a keyboard user would use.
items.reference:
🔊 Screen reader — reads the accessibility tree aloud
🕹️ Switch device — single/few-button navigation
🗣️ Voice control — spoken commands to operate the UI

items.prompt:
A `
Save
` and a `` look pixel-identical after styling. What is different about them for a keyboard-only user, by default?
choices: Nothing — once CSS styling makes them look and feel identical, the browser treats both elements as equivalent for focus and keyboard purposes
The `<div>` is not in the default Tab order and has no keyboard activation, while `<button>` gets both for free
The `<button>` only becomes Tab-reachable once an onclick handler is attached via JavaScript, same as the `<div>` needs tabindex added
The `<div>` is reachable by Tab automatically whenever it has an onclick handler, while `<button>` needs an explicit tabindex to work
items.explanation: Native interactive elements like `<button>` are focusable and keyboard-activatable (Enter and Space) automatically. A `<div>` has none of that by default — it needs `tabindex`, a role, and manual keydown handling to match.
items.reference:
<div onclick>
role: generic (nothing)
<button>
role: button (free)

Why: the browser computes role/focus/keyboard handling for native elements automatically.

items.prompt: To make a `<div onclick>` fully equivalent to a native `<button>` for keyboard and screen reader users, which of these is NOT actually required?
choices: `tabindex="0"` so it's reachable by Tab
`role="button"` so its role is announced
A `background-color` matching the design system's brand color
A keydown handler so both Enter and Space activate it
items.explanation: Visual styling like background-color has no bearing on accessibility — it's purely cosmetic. Tab reachability, an explicit role, and keyboard activation (Enter and Space) are the actual functional requirements a native button provides automatically.
items.reference:
<div onclick>
role: generic (nothing)
<button>
role: button (free)

Why: the browser computes role/focus/keyboard handling for native elements automatically.

items.prompt: Why does L2 recommend defaulting to native HTML elements over ARIA-patched `<div>`s wherever a native equivalent exists?
choices: Because ARIA attributes have been deprecated in favor of a newer attribute set, so patched `<div>`s using the old ARIA roles will stop working in upcoming browser versions
Because native elements get role, keyboard focus, and keyboard activation from the browser automatically, while a `<div>` requires every one of those to be added and maintained by hand
Because `<div>` elements are not permitted inside `<form>` tags under the HTML living standard, which forces custom widgets to use semantic elements instead
Because ARIA role support was only ever implemented in one browser engine, so relying on ARIA-patched `<div>`s breaks accessibility everywhere else
items.explanation: A native element's accessible behavior is built into the browser and can't be forgotten. A manually-patched `<div>` depends on every required piece — tabindex, role, keydown handling — being added correctly and never regressing.
items.reference:
<div onclick>
role: generic (nothing)
<button>
role: button (free)

Why: the browser computes role/focus/keyboard handling for native elements automatically.

items.prompt: A screen reader announces 'Save, button.' Where does that announcement come from?
choices: The element's CSS class name, since screen readers try to infer meaning from class and id attributes
The accessibility tree, computed from the DOM as role + accessible name + state
The page's `<title>` tag text, repeated for every element a screen reader encounters on the page
The browser's bookmark title, if the page happens to already be saved in the user's bookmarks
items.explanation: The browser builds a separate accessibility tree alongside the DOM, computing role, accessible name, and state for each element. Screen readers read that tree, never CSS and not the raw HTML directly.
items.reference:
HTML → Accessibility tree → Screen reader

Why: assistive tech reads the computed tree (role/name/state), never the raw HTML or CSS directly.

items.prompt: Does the CSS used to visually style an element ever get read by a screen reader?
choices: Yes — screen readers parse the computed CSS and announce color names and font families as part of describing each element
No — CSS affects visual presentation only; the accessibility tree is computed from the DOM, not CSS
Only if the style uses `!important`, since that flag marks the rule as significant enough to expose to the accessibility tree
Only for `background-color`, because that property is treated as semantic shading information rather than pure decoration
items.explanation: CSS controls what something looks like, not what it structurally is. The accessibility tree — role, name, state — is computed from the DOM/HTML, and CSS plays no part in that computation.
items.reference:
HTML → Accessibility tree → Screen reader

Why: assistive tech reads the computed tree (role/name/state), never the raw HTML or CSS directly.

items.prompt: What does 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' mean in practice?
choices: ARIA attributes should never be used under any circumstances, since native HTML elements can always be restyled to look exactly like any custom widget a design calls for
Adding a role like `role="button"` without also implementing the keyboard behavior real buttons have is worse than leaving the element unmarked, because it falsely promises that behavior
ARIA only matters for mobile apps, not websites, because desktop screen readers rely entirely on native HTML semantics and ignore ARIA roles
ARIA attributes slow down page load significantly, since the browser has to parse and validate each role against the full ARIA specification at runtime
items.explanation: An ARIA role is a contract about behavior, not just a label. Claiming `role="button"` without keyboard activation tells assistive tech (and the user) it behaves like a button, then fails to deliver — a worse experience than no claim at all.
items.reference:
Adding a role without the matching keyboard behavior is a broken promise, not a partial win

Why: ARIA roles announce a contract about behavior — the behavior still has to be built.

items.prompt: A custom dropdown is built from styled `<div>`/`<span>` elements with `role="listbox"` and `role="option"` added, but no keyboard handling was implemented. What happens for a screen reader user?
choices: Nothing changes for the user — ARIA roles only affect how the element is described in developer tools, not what a screen reader actually announces
The screen reader announces it as a fully interactive listbox, setting an expectation that arrow-key navigation and selection will work — which then fails
The browser automatically adds matching keyboard handling once it detects a `role="listbox"` attribute in the markup
The dropdown becomes completely invisible to the screen reader, since an element can't carry a role without full keyboard support already in place
items.explanation: The roles make the accessibility tree claim full listbox behavior, which the screen reader announces. When the promised keyboard interaction isn't implemented, the user gets a confident announcement followed by nothing working as described.
items.reference:
Adding a role without the matching keyboard behavior is a broken promise, not a partial win

Why: ARIA roles announce a contract about behavior — the behavior still has to be built.

items.prompt: When is reaching for an ARIA role the right call, per L2?
choices: Always — adding ARIA roles to every element, native or custom, is considered a best practice that makes the markup more explicit
When there's no native HTML element that already provides the needed role, name, and behavior, such as a custom tab panel
Only on elements that are already visually hidden, since ARIA exists specifically to describe content sighted users can't see
Never — native elements should always be used even for genuinely custom widgets
items.explanation: ARIA exists specifically to describe custom widgets with no native equivalent (tab panels, comboboxes). Where a native element already does the job, ARIA is unnecessary and adds a maintenance burden the browser would otherwise handle for free.
items.reference:
Adding a role without the matching keyboard behavior is a broken promise, not a partial win

Why: ARIA roles announce a contract about behavior — the behavior still has to be built.

items.prompt: Why does 'try using only the keyboard, no mouse' catch both keyboard-accessibility bugs and many screen-reader bugs at the same time?
choices: It doesn't — keyboard accessibility and screen reader compatibility are tested completely separately and rarely share the same underlying bugs
Because screen reader users also navigate primarily with Tab, Shift+Tab, and arrow keys rather than a mouse, so anything mouse-only breaks for both groups
Because screen readers automatically disable the mouse the moment they're turned on, forcing every interaction through the keyboard instead
Because keyboard-only testing only reveals visual CSS bugs like missing focus outlines, not deeper markup or structural problems
items.explanation: Screen reader users move focus with the keyboard, not a mouse. An interaction that only fires on `mouseover`/`click` with no keyboard equivalent is invisible to a keyboard-only user and a screen reader user for the identical underlying reason.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Can you reach it? (Tab order)
2️⃣ Can you tell where focus is? (visible outline)
3️⃣ Can you escape it? (no keyboard trap)

Why: screen reader users navigate by keyboard too — this test catches both keyboard and screen-reader bugs at once.

items.prompt: A developer removes the default focus outline with `outline: none` in CSS to match a design mockup, without adding a replacement style. What accessibility problem does this cause?
choices: None — the focus outline is purely a decorative flourish, not something any user relies on
Keyboard users lose the only visual cue for where focus currently is on the page
It breaks screen readers entirely, since they read the outline's position to announce focus
It only affects users on Safari, since other browsers draw a focus indicator regardless of the CSS
items.explanation: The focus outline is how a sighted keyboard user tracks where they are on the page. Removing it with nothing in its place leaves them tabbing through invisible focus with no way to tell what's currently selected.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Can you reach it? (Tab order)
2️⃣ Can you tell where focus is? (visible outline)
3️⃣ Can you escape it? (no keyboard trap)

Why: screen reader users navigate by keyboard too — this test catches both keyboard and screen-reader bugs at once.

items.prompt: A settings panel opens as an overlay, and once focus enters it, Tab cycles endlessly among the panel's own controls with no way to reach the rest of the page. What is this called?
choices: A keyboard trap
Focus restoration
A tab index
A modal dialog (this is expected behavior)
items.explanation: A keyboard trap is when a keyboard-only user can enter a region of the page but has no keyboard path back out of it — WCAG treats this as a serious failure since it can leave the user stuck with no way to reach anything else on the page.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Can you reach it? (Tab order)
2️⃣ Can you tell where focus is? (visible outline)
3️⃣ Can you escape it? (no keyboard trap)

Why: screen reader users navigate by keyboard too — this test catches both keyboard and screen-reader bugs at once.

items.prompt: Which markup correctly and permanently associates a visible label with its input field?
choices: `<input type="text" placeholder="Email" />` (text vanishes once typing starts)
`<label for="email">Email</label><input type="text" id="email" />`
`Email` (no programmatic link between them)
`<input type="text" title="Email" />` (tooltip only, not a real label)
items.explanation: A `<label>` with `for` pointing to the input's matching `id` creates a real, permanent, programmatic association that assistive tech can rely on — unlike placeholder text, a nearby `<span>`, or a `title` attribute, none of which reliably serve as a label.
items.reference:
placeholder="Email"
vanishes once typing starts
<label for="email">
always visible, always associated

items.prompt: An accessible name's lookup order checks `aria-label` first. If a button already has clear visible text ('Submit') and someone also adds `aria-label="Send form"`, what happens?
choices: Nothing — visible text content always takes priority over `aria-label` in every browser's accessible-name computation
The `aria-label` overrides the visible text for screen reader users, so they hear 'Send form' while sighted users see 'Submit' — a mismatch
The button becomes inaccessible entirely, since having both visible text and an `aria-label` creates a conflict the accessibility tree can't resolve
Both texts get announced together, back to back, so screen reader users hear 'Submit, Send form' as one combined announcement
items.explanation: `aria-label` wins outright over visible text content in the accessible-name lookup order. Adding one alongside clear visible text can create a confusing mismatch between what's seen and what's announced.
items.reference:
placeholder="Email"
vanishes once typing starts
<label for="email">
always visible, always associated

items.prompt: In the audit, the error text's color changed from `#f28b8b` (2.3:1) to `#c02626` (5.9:1) on a white background. What else about the markup changed to fix the contrast failure?
choices:
The element's tag changed from `

` to `` for the new color
Nothing — it was purely a color value change, same DOM structure
An `aria-label` describing the error's severity was also added
The font size was increased a few pixels alongside the color
items.explanation:
The contrast fix in the audit was purely a CSS color change on the same `

` element — no DOM/markup change was needed. Contrast is a visual-luminance property, not a structural one.
items.reference:
ColorsRatioAA?
#f28b8b on #fff2.3:1Fails
#c02626 on #fff5.9:1Passes

items.prompt: Why did the original error color (`#f28b8b`, a light red) fail contrast even though it visually reads as an intentional 'error' color?
choices: Because red as a hue is inherently inaccessible for error text, regardless of exactly which shade or luminance value is chosen, so no red ever passes contrast
Because a color can look intentional and on-brand while still being too close in luminance to the background — 'looks like an error color' and 'has enough contrast' are unrelated properties
Because WCAG requires all error states to sit on a black background specifically, and the light background was the actual cause of the failure
Because the text was rendered at too small a font size, and font size — not color — is what actually determines a contrast ratio calculation
items.explanation: Contrast measures a mathematical luminance difference, not stylistic intent. A light, friendly-looking red can still fail the ratio the same way any other light color can — checking the actual ratio is the only reliable way to know.
items.reference:
ColorsRatioAA?
#f28b8b on #fff2.3:1Fails
#c02626 on #fff5.9:1Passes

items.prompt: Level AA requires a 4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text. A design has text at exactly 4.5:1. Per the reasoning in L2/L3, is this a safe choice?
choices: Yes, it clears the minimum exactly, and WCAG ratios are precise enough that hitting 4.5:1 on the nose carries no practical risk
It's a legitimate pass but a fragile one — any small variance in rendering or display quality could tip it below the threshold in practice
No, it always fails in real browsers regardless of the calculation
It only matters for AAA, not AA, since AA's 4.5:1 figure is a recommended target rather than an enforced minimum
items.explanation: A ratio right at the threshold is a real pass but has zero margin — a slightly different gamma correction, low-quality display, or near-identical color pick could push it below 4.5:1 in practice, even though the calculation says it clears the line today.
items.reference:
ColorsRatioAA?
#f28b8b on #fff2.3:1Fails
#c02626 on #fff5.9:1Passes

items.prompt: In the audit's modal finding, Tab moved focus out of the open modal into the page content behind it. What was missing from the original markup that allowed this?
choices: A `z-index` value high enough to visually sit above the page content behind the modal overlay
`role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`, plus focus management keeping Tab inside the dialog while open
A `<form>` wrapper around the modal's contents, which browsers use to contain Tab navigation
A larger close button, sized so it's easier to find and dismiss the modal before Tab reaches the page behind it
items.explanation: The overlay looked blocking to a sighted mouse user because of CSS z-index and a backdrop, but nothing told the accessibility tree the region outside the modal was inert, and no focus management kept keyboard navigation contained — so Tab moved straight into the page behind it.
items.reference:
role="dialog" — what it is
aria-modal="true" — everything outside is inert
aria-labelledby — dialog's own accessible name

Why: markup declares intent; focus movement and Escape still have to be implemented separately.

items.prompt: Adding `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` to the modal's markup was one part of the fix. Was that alone sufficient to fully fix the keyboard behavior?
choices: Yes, ARIA attributes alone implement all necessary keyboard behavior — the browser reads `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal` and automatically contains focus, no extra script needed

No — the markup declares the intended behavior, but focus still had to be moved into the dialog on open, kept inside via Tab/Shift+Tab, and returned to the trigger button on Escape, all implemented separately
No, because `aria-modal` is not a real ARIA attribute at all, so it was silently ignored and contributed nothing to the fix the audit described
Yes, because `role="dialog"` automatically disables the rest of the page and moves focus for you, without any additional script required
items.explanation: ARIA attributes describe what an element is, not how it behaves — the actual focus movement (into the dialog on open, contained by Tab/Shift+Tab, restored to the trigger on Escape) is behavior that still has to be built, same as the ARIA-role lesson from L2.
items.reference:
role="dialog" — what it is
aria-modal="true" — everything outside is inert
aria-labelledby — dialog's own accessible name

Why: markup declares intent; focus movement and Escape still have to be implemented separately.

items.prompt: The audit's close button had an SVG icon and no text anywhere. What did the screen reader announce before the fix, and why exactly that?
choices: "Close, button" — screen readers read an SVG's internal filename or asset path as its accessible name by default
"button" only — role was present (native `<button>`), but the accessible-name lookup ran out of places to look and found nothing
Nothing at all — the button was completely invisible to the screen reader
"Icon, button" — any `<svg>` element with no attributes defaults to the generic accessible name 'icon' in every browser
items.explanation: The native `<button>` still had a role. But with no `aria-label`, no `aria-labelledby`, and no text content (an SVG's path data isn't text), the name lookup found nothing — leaving just the bare role announced.
items.reference:
Before: "button"
After: "Close, button"

Why: role alone announces nothing useful without an accessible name to go with it.

items.prompt: After the fix, the close button gained `aria-label="Close"` and the SVG inside it gained `aria-hidden="true"`. What does `aria-hidden="true"` accomplish here specifically?
choices: It visually hides the icon from sighted users entirely, which is why the button also needed visible text content as a replacement
It stops the screen reader from attempting to describe the decorative SVG's raw path data as if it were meaningful content
It disables the button for keyboard users, since `aria-hidden` removes the whole element from the Tab order along with the accessibility tree
It's required syntax that `aria-label` depends on to work at all, but has no functional effect of its own on what's announced
items.explanation: `aria-hidden="true"` removes an element from the accessibility tree entirely. The icon stays visible on screen for sighted users, but a screen reader skips it — appropriate since the icon is purely decorative once `aria-label` already supplies the name.
items.reference:
Before: "button"
After: "Close, button"

Why: role alone announces nothing useful without an accessible name to go with it.

items.prompt: Why might visible text reading 'Close' next to the icon be a better fix than `aria-label="Close"` alone, per the audit's reasoning?
choices: `aria-label` doesn't actually work in most browsers, which already forced the team to rely on visible text as the only reliable option
`aria-label` only helps screen reader users — it does nothing for sighted users with low vision who can't interpret the icon glyph itself
Visible text is required by WCAG Level A for every button, while `aria-label` alone only satisfies the less strict Level AA criterion
There's no difference; they're equally good in every situation, since both ultimately resolve to the same accessible name either way
items.explanation: `aria-label` fixes the announcement for screen reader users only. Someone with low vision who can see a button exists but can't interpret a small `×` glyph gets no benefit from an attribute that isn't visually rendered.
items.reference:
Before: "button"
After: "Close, button"

Why: role alone announces nothing useful without an accessible name to go with it.

items.prompt: A form's error text appears dynamically via JavaScript after a failed submit, with no `aria-live` region involved. Will a screen reader user reliably hear the new error text without moving focus?
choices: Yes, any text that gets inserted into the DOM is automatically picked up and announced by whichever screen reader is currently running
Not reliably — a plain DOM update with no `aria-live` region isn't guaranteed to be announced unless focus moves to it or it's marked as a live region
Yes, but only in Chrome, since other browsers don't expose dynamic DOM changes to their accessibility APIs at all
No, dynamic content can never be made accessible to screen readers no matter how it's marked up or when focus is moved
items.explanation: Screen readers don't automatically announce every DOM change. Content that appears without a focus change needs to be inside an `aria-live` region (or receive focus directly) to reliably be announced.
items.reference:
Static text change ≠ automatically announced
aria-live="polite" — announced when the user is idle
aria-live="assertive" — interrupts immediately

items.prompt: What is the practical difference between `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-live="assertive"`?
choices: There is no difference; both values are just alternate spellings for the exact same live-region announcement behavior
"polite" waits until the screen reader is idle before announcing; "assertive" interrupts whatever is currently being read
"assertive" is reserved for image alt-text updates, while "polite" is reserved for plain text content changes
"polite" only works inside button elements, while "assertive" is restricted to form field updates specifically
items.explanation: "polite" queues the announcement until the user's current reading finishes — appropriate for most status updates. "assertive" interrupts immediately, reserved for urgent, time-sensitive information since it disrupts whatever the user was doing.
items.reference:
Static text change ≠ automatically announced
aria-live="polite" — announced when the user is idle
aria-live="assertive" — interrupts immediately

items.prompt: WCAG's target-size guidance (2.5.5) recommends a minimum interactive target size of roughly:
choices: 16×16 CSS pixels

items.prompt: Why does target size matter specifically for users with a tremor or limited fine motor control, beyond general usability?
